passage: Rehana, sit. You're nervous about Monday's viva, I can see it. Let me tell you about mine. I was twenty, in Aligarh, in a room with three professors and one creaking ceiling fan. The first question was easy, about soil. And my mind went white, like a slate wiped clean. My hands were stuck to my knees and my throat was dry. The longest silence of my life. Then I remembered my father saying, when you are frightened, breathe out longer than you breathe in. So I did, twice. And I said it aloud: "Forgive me, my mind has gone blank. May I start again?" The oldest professor nodded. "Take your time, Miss Parveen." The words came back slowly, like water into a well. I passed, Rehana. Your Nani passed.

qa.q: How many professors were in the room at Parveen's viva?
qa.a: Three professors, with one creaking ceiling fan.

qa.q: What did Parveen feel when the mind went white?
qa.a: Parveen felt frozen with fear: hands stuck to the knees, a dry throat and a silence that felt endless.

qa.q: What turning point let Parveen answer again?
qa.a: Parveen breathed out longer than in, twice, and admitted aloud to going blank, which let the freeze thaw.

qa.q: How might the oldest professor have seen Parveen's silence?
qa.a: The professor seemed to see a nervous student rather than an unprepared one, and gave Parveen time to start again.

grounding: A young adult's mind goes blank in a viva, and slowing the breath and naming the moment aloud help it pass.

passage: Manoj had his bag on his shoulder and a train in forty minutes. "Thomas, the electricity bill. Three weeks now. Are you paying or not?" Out in the hostel corridor someone's speaker was booming, and every word Thomas had rehearsed disappeared. His jaw locked. His arms went stiff at his sides. He had lost his part-time shift and had only half the money, but his mouth wouldn't open. Manoj sighed loudly. Thomas pressed his feet into the floor and let one slow breath out, then another. "Sorry, I've frozen up," he said. "I've got half now. Can I pay the rest on Friday?" Manoj's shoulders dropped. "Why didn't you just say that?" "I couldn't, for a second." Manoj nodded and ran for his train.

qa.q: How long did Manoj have before his train?
qa.a: Manoj had a train in forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when his jaw locked?
qa.a: Thomas was overwhelmed and afraid; the rehearsed words vanished and his body went stiff.
Thomas pressed his feet into the floor, let out slow breaths and named the freeze aloud, then offered a clear plan for the money.

qa.q: How might Manoj have read Thomas's silence before Thomas spoke?
qa.a: Manoj may have taken it as dodging the bill, which is why he sighed loudly, until Thomas explained.

grounding: A young adult goes blank and stiff in a tense argument, and slowing the breath and naming the moment let him speak again.
